title: Hand knob sign in osmotic demyelinating syndrome
case_prompt: A 44-year-old previously healthy woman was referred for evaluation of bilateral hand weakness. Five weeks earlier, she had a motorcycle accident with transient loss of consciousness. Initial head CT was unremarkable, and she underwent internal fixation of a right medial malleolar fracture under spinal anesthesia. On the first postoperative day, she received 5% dextrose in 0.9% saline, and on hospital day six she experienced headache and vomiting managed with 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline and antiemetics. Repeat head CT on hospital day seven was normal. One week after discharge, her family noticed episodes of uncontrollable laughter and crying without context, associated with generalized weakness and fatigue. On exam, she had a pseudobulbar affect, normal strength (grade V) in all muscle groups, and hyperreflexia. Her serum sodium was 140 mmol/L. Brain MRI showed symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the bilateral caudate and putamen with corresponding diffusion-weighted imaging hyperintensity. Cerebrospinal fluid studies, including meningitis/encephalitis and autoimmune encephalitis panels, anti–aquaporin-4, anti-MOG, and antinuclear antibodies, were negative. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the upper extremities were unremarkable except for poor activation on maximal effort. A cervical spine MRI showed mild spinal canal stenosis, which was insufficient to explain her bilateral hand weakness.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Extrapontine myelinolysis is likely given the symmetric deep grey–white matter changes — “These findings were suggestive of extrapontine myelinolysis.”  
2. Infectious or autoimmune encephalitis is unlikely because extensive CSF and serum panels were negative — “All panel and immunologic studies were negative.”  
3. Peripheral neuropathy was excluded by normal nerve conduction and EMG studies — “The nerve conduction study and electromyography ... were unremarkable ... This suggests an upper motor neuron lesion as the cause of bilateral hand weakness.”  
4. Cervical myelopathy is insufficient to explain bilateral hand weakness because only mild stenosis was noted — “A cervical spine MRI showed mild spinal canal stenosis, which was insufficient to explain the bilateral hand weakness.”  
5. Ischemic stroke of the hand knob area may cause isolated hand weakness but typically presents as a focal cortical infarct, not symmetric basal ganglia lesions — “Hand weakness ... has been described as an atypical presentation of ischemic stroke with selective infarction in the hand knob area.”  
6. Brain metastases involving the hand motor cortex could produce hand weakness but are usually mass lesions rather than diffuse symmetric hyperintensities — “as well as brain metastasis in the hand motor cortex.”
